doc.title: John Best interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Favorite years, Little Bavaria and Billy May and Matty Matlock
summary: Little Bavaria jazz nights, Matlock recordings, and Billy May's Time-Life dates.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: When you look back on your career in music, would you say that there’s a few years that you really look fondly on, because of the band you were in or just because of the success of the music at that time? What was your favorite years in the music career?
Well that’s tough. It would have to be I think more recent than the original three.

Because I’ve done, for about ten years my late wife and I put on jazz things right at a place called Little Bavaria. And there, we just took over the place and hired the musicians. Most of them were like Nick Fatool, Eddie Miller and Abe Most, and Abe © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

Lincoln the trombone player, and Bobby Gordon. All good jazz players, and that went on once a month for about ten years. And I think as far as — of course I was the leader, so I got to do what I picked. But working with Matty Matlock, who did a lot of recordings, and he used me on, those are the things that I’m glad I did because I can listen to those — they’re not like the big organized bands, it’s just a recording date, you do that and you don’t play that, but Matty was a wonderful writer, arranger, a good clarinet player. And also Billy May. Billy May was probably my best friend in the whole music business. When I first came to Hollywood he gave me my first recording dates and we did the Time-Life series. I can remember when I was in Palma Valley, that’s where the orchard was, I wasn’t playing very much and Billy used to come down and he said “how’s your lip?” or something like that. Well it wasn’t too good, I said — I don’t think I should have — because these dates are pretty hard. So for a while there I didn’t think I was up to it. So he came down once and I was doing an ice show in San Diego, I was really working on it. So he says, “How’s your lip?” I said, “Well I just did the ice show.” “Well do you want to do some recording?” I said, “Yeah.” So that’s what it was with the Time-Life thing. And that thing went on for, well there were fifteen albums, copies, all these were copies of the original records you know. I started on the third album I think. But that lasted like maybe a couple of years.
